explanations.answer: The Nile is mine and I made it myself
explanations.explanation: That's his brag, friend. God quotes Pharaoh: “The Nile is mine; I made it myself.” (Ezek 29:3) That's like me strutting around claiming I baked the whole batch when the oven did all the heavy lifting. The oven would NOT sign off on that.

explanations.answer: The Nile was handed to me by my gods
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but that's not his line. In the words God quotes, Pharaoh never mentions anyone handing him anything. He says, “The Nile is mine; I made it myself.” (Ezek 29:3) The credit goes straight to himself.

explanations.answer: The Nile will flow forever just for me
explanations.explanation: That's a bold brag, but it isn't the one in the verse. Pharaoh talks about owning the Nile and making it, and nothing about it flowing forever. His words are: “The Nile is mine; I made it myself.” (Ezek 29:3) Claiming you made a whole river is plenty.

The fish of his streams, baker. God says, “the fish of your streams will cling to your scales.” (Ezek 29:4) It's like crumbs stuck to my apron, only these are fish stuck to scales. And God says it twice in that one verse, so the picture is clear.
Mud sounds right for a riverbank, but this verse never mentions it. God says, “the fish of your streams will cling to your scales.” (Ezek 29:4) The fish are what come up with him.
Frogs would make this a much noisier haul, friend. But the verse doesn't have them. God says, “the fish of your streams will cling to your scales.” (Ezek 29:4)
It's the opposite, friend. God says Pharaoh “will not be taken away or gathered for burial.” (Ezek 29:5) I think this is a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly and let it be heavy.

That's right, friend. God says Pharaoh “will not be taken away or gathered for burial.” (Ezek 29:5) He also says He has given him as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air. I think this is a hard one to read, so I'll say it plainly and move on.

That's the whole point, baker. God says, “Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD.” (Ezek 29:6) That line comes back in verse 9 and again in verse 21. God wants this message to land.

explanations.answer: That their gods have left them
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but the verse never says it. What the people of Egypt will know is this: “that I am the LORD.” (Ezek 29:6) The focus is on who God is, not on anyone leaving.

explanations.answer: That their king has run away
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Pharaoh running anywhere, friend. God says He'll haul him up and leave him in the desert (Ezek 29:4-5). And what all Egypt will know is “that I am the LORD.” (Ezek 29:6)

Reeds, baker. God says Egypt was “only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel.” (Ezek 29:6) A reed might look like a walking stick, but try putting your weight on it. It's like using a drinking straw for a cane.
Cedar sounds like it would hold up, and that's exactly why it doesn't fit. God calls Egypt “only a staff of reeds.” (Ezek 29:6) Verse 7 shows how that staff goes: it splintered and broke.
Nobody splinters an iron staff, friend. The picture is the opposite of that. God says Egypt was “only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel.” (Ezek 29:6)

explanations.answer: It splinters and tears their shoulders
explanations.explanation: That's what happens, baker. God says, “you splintered, tearing all their shoulders” (Ezek 29:7). A reed staff gives out right when you need it. Ouch.

explanations.answer: It holds but bends down low
explanations.explanation: A reed that holds would be nice, friend, but that's not the picture. God says that when Israel took hold of it, “you splintered, tearing all their shoulders” (Ezek 29:7). It didn't hold.

explanations.answer: It sinks into the soft mud
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't take us into mud, baker. It stays right in their hands and on their shoulders. God says, “you splintered, tearing all their shoulders” (Ezek 29:7).

True, friend, and this one is heavy. God says, “I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast.” (Ezek 29:8) The verse begins with “Therefore,” so it follows from what came before. I'll say it straight and not joke about it.

This one is actually true, friend, and it's a heavy verse. God says, “I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast.” (Ezek 29:8) The verse begins with “Therefore,” so it follows from what came before. I'll just say it plainly.

Rivers, baker. God says, “therefore I am against you and against your rivers.” (Ezek 29:10) Pharaoh bragged about the Nile in verse 9, and the verse says that's why. Brag about a river and the river ends up in the sentence.
Chariots sound like a fair guess, but they aren't in this verse. God says, “therefore I am against you and against your rivers.” (Ezek 29:10) The brag was about the Nile, so the rivers come up.
No priests in this verse, friend. After the Nile brag, God says, “therefore I am against you and against your rivers.” (Ezek 29:10) It stays on the water.

explanations.answer: No man or beast will pass through
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God says, “No foot of man or beast will pass through” (Ezek 29:11). That's a road with zero traffic, and not one GPS voice saying "recalculating."
Not even shepherds, friend. The verse says, “No foot of man or beast will pass through” (Ezek 29:11). Nobody gets named as an exception.
Traders don't get a pass in this verse, baker. God says, “No foot of man or beast will pass through” (Ezek 29:11). That leaves nobody on the list.

Half of it is right, friend. The land is uninhabited for forty years (Ezek 29:11). But the Egyptians don't stay put. God says, “I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries.” (Ezek 29:12)

That's right, baker. The land sits uninhabited for forty years (Ezek 29:11), and the Egyptians aren't in it. God says, “I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries.” (Ezek 29:12) Forty years is a long stretch to be away.

explanations.answer: Gather them back from the nations
explanations.explanation: That's what God says, baker. “At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered.” (Ezek 29:13) The scattering has an end date. God sets it Himself.

The verse goes the other way, friend. God says, “At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered.” (Ezek 29:13) The scattering doesn't last forever.

Servants to Israel isn't anywhere in this verse, baker. What God says is, “At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered.” (Ezek 29:13) Gathering is what He promises.
Lowly, friend. God says of Egypt in Pathros, “There they will be a lowly kingdom.” (Ezek 29:14) They get a place to live, but a humble spot on the map.
Mighty doesn't match, baker. God says, “There they will be a lowly kingdom.” (Ezek 29:14) And verse 15 calls Egypt “the lowliest of kingdoms.”
The verse says nothing about dividing, friend. It says, “There they will be a lowly kingdom.” (Ezek 29:14) The word to remember is lowly.

It's the other way around, baker. God says Egypt “will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations.” (Ezek 29:15) He adds, “I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations.” That's two ways of saying the same thing.

That's right, friend. God says Egypt “will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations.” (Ezek 29:15) He also says, “I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations.” Egypt isn't getting that crown back.

explanations.answer: Their sin in turning to Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says Egypt “will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians.” (Ezek 29:16) Egypt stops being something to lean on and becomes a reminder.

explanations.answer: Their years as slaves in Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's not what this verse points to, friend. It says Egypt “will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians.” (Ezek 29:16) The reminder is about Israel turning to Egypt.

explanations.answer: Their escape across the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: The sea isn't in this verse, baker. God says Egypt “will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians.” (Ezek 29:16) That's the reminder He names.

It's the opposite, friend. The verse says, “But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it.” (Ezek 29:18) That's the sinking feeling of checking your bank account on payday and finding nothing there.

That's right, baker. “But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it.” (Ezek 29:18) All that work, and no pay from Tyre. That's the sinking feeling of checking your bank account on payday and finding nothing there.
Egypt, friend. God says, “I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon” (Ezek 29:19). Tyre is the city he worked against in verse 18, but the land handed to him is Egypt.
Wages, baker. God says, “This will be the wages for his army.” (Ezek 29:19) After the work in verse 18 with no wages from Tyre, I think this is a payday that finally shows up.
Tyre is in the story, friend, but it's not the land being given. Verse 18 says Nebuchadnezzar and his army received no wages from Tyre. The land God gives him is Egypt (Ezek 29:19).
Edom doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, baker. The land God names for Nebuchadnezzar is Egypt (Ezek 29:19). Keep your eye on the names in the verse.
Ransom sounds like a heist movie, friend. But God's word here is wages: “This will be the wages for his army.” (Ezek 29:19) It's pay for the work.

explanations.answer: Because the labor was done for God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives, baker. He says, “I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me” (Ezek 29:20). The text states the reason plainly.

explanations.answer: Because Babylon begged God for it
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage says Babylon begged, friend. The reason God gives is, “because it was done for Me” (Ezek 29:20). That's all the verse says on the matter.
The passage doesn't say Egypt attacked anybody, baker. God gives His reason in verse 20: “because it was done for Me”. That's the reason in the text.

True, friend. God tells Ezekiel, “I will open your mouth to speak among them.” (Ezek 29:21) Ezekiel is the one God has been calling “Son of man” (Ezek 29:18). A mouth opened and a message to speak? I'd be doing a happy dance on my gold base.

It's actually in there, baker. God says, “I will open your mouth to speak among them.” (Ezek 29:21) He's speaking to Ezekiel, the one He's been calling “Son of man” (Ezek 29:18). That promise is part of the last verse.
